newsitem.title: UK: Staid British campaign ignites over Europe.
newsitem.headline: Staid British campaign ignites over Europe.

text.p: Henry V had his Agincourt, Winston Churchill battled the Germans and Margaret Thatcher took on all comers to fight Britain's corner in Europe.
Now Europe has brought out the fighter in Prime Minister John Major too -- and finally injected some passion into an election campaign that that has veered from dry to trite.

In some of the most gripping theatre of the entire campaign, Major launched an ardent defence of his stance on a single currency on Wednesday, seeking to still revolt in his own party and stage a come-from-behind victory in the May 1 election.
Speaking with unusual eloquence, Major explained in detail why his stance on joining the single currency -- basically a decision to decide later -- was the only policy that made sense.
Many on his right want Major to rule out membership forever, even though he has limped ever closer to their Euro-sceptic line by saying membership looks unlikely in the first wave of 1999.
To rule out joining altogether, years before monetary union even began, he said, would be like entering a poker game naked, his cards faced upwards for all the world to see.
"Like me or loathe me, do not bind my hands when I am negotiating on behalf of the British nation," said Major.
"I will negotiate in the interests of the United Kingdom as a whole, not in the convenient party political interests of the Conservative party," he told a news conference.
It was Major at his best: combative yet jokey, driven but not dogmatic and designed to show he was in control of his party even as they peel off one by one over Europe.

After weeks of sleaze and sex scandals, sound bites, fringe candidates and grown men dressed as symbolic chickens, his gutsy performance and command of the detail was a welcome injection of grit into a campaign short of substance and energy.
It also showed how much things had changed.

For while Europe has traditionally been a contentious topic in Britain, elections used to be largely set-piece battles between Labour and the Conservatives, who engaged in worthy debate about left versus right and rich versus poor.
Now the gap between the major parties has grown so narrow that the old markers no longer work, allowing intra-party divisions to spill to the surface.

Major set out his European stall only after two ministers broke with his carefully crafted compromise on monetary union: a compromise that was supposed to avert internal squabbling in the run-up to the election.
Major publicly rebuked the pair but they survived, leading to new taunts that he was weak and his party rudderless.
"We are witnessing the collapse of the Conservative Party under the weight of its own divisions," said Labour leader Tony Blair, who is widely expected to win the election.
"Britain cannot be represented by a government with all the leadership qualities of lemmings."

For it is members of Major's own party -- not the opposition or the public -- who have a problem with the premier's views on Europe, and Major's bravura showing was expected to win few converts among his die-hard Euro-sceptic colleagues.
"I feel sorry for Mr Major," crowed Blair, double digits ahead in the polls. "He's got a very difficult situation because his party is virtually incapable of being led properly."

While Major and Blair -- both cautious over monetary union -- face equal dissent over Europe, it is Major who cannot contain his critics, despite the fact it is Labour that traditionally rips itself apart over principles.

"This is not a division between the Conservative and the Labour parties on Europe. We both share the same view that options should remain open. The division between the Conservatives and the Labour Party is one of leadership," said Gordon Brown, Labour's economics spokesman.
